narrative:
The model predicts you have a 12% chance of failing your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, zero past failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of traits the model sees this clean record as less protective than it appears. 

The second strongest influence is your weekly study time of more than 10 hours. This is very unusual—only 3.4% of students who passed studied this much—yet the model still interprets it as pushing you slightly toward failing. It seems the system believes that even with this heavy investment, other parts of your profile are not aligning for success.

Finally, the fact that you receive extra educational support at school ranks third. While almost all students who passed did not need this help (only 3.4% did), your use of school support is read by the model as a signal that tilts the outcome toward failure.

To improve, focus on making your long study hours more effective, perhaps by changing how you revise or seeking feedback on your methods. Talk to your teachers about whether the extra support is truly helping or if a different approach would be better. Small adjustments in study quality and support could shift your trajectory before the final exams. (248 words)
